findings.F1: The tested result points the way the idea predicts but falls short of the bar: the mean excess 2-day return over all folds is +0.22 % (t 0.51, 463 cases on 191 days, slope t 0.33). On folds B and C the same cases (one per 2-day cell, 20-day z ≤ −2) give +1.23 % over 2 days and +1.24 % over 1 day, but with cases on one day taken together the t is only 1.55 and 1.43, because the 184 cases fall on only 74 days.
findings.F2: The effect lasts 1 to 2 days and then fades. The excess return is +1.24 % (naive t 2.53) over 1 day and +1.23 % (t 2.52) over 2 days, then +0.44 % (t 0.67) over 3 days and −0.56 % (t −0.60) over 5 days, so the plan's 2-day horizon is where the effect shows.
findings.F3: The effect is mixed across periods and is drowned in one of them.
findings.F4: The rise is positive on every coin but significant on none. The 2-day means run from +0.46 % (ETH, t 0.41) to +1.98 % (XRP, t 1.34), with 25 to 35 cases per coin, so each coin adds too few cases on its own.
findings.F5: The grading is weak and not monotone, which is why the slope fails.
findings.F6: No split by trend explains the result.
findings.F7: In size the move is close to the cost of a trade. The unusual move of +0.22 % per case is 1.2 times the 0.19 % round-trip cost, with a strength of 0.037 of a usual 2-day move (6.58 %).

ideas.name: sharp fall rebound, more coins
ideas.idea: When a coin's daily return is a fall that is large against its own typical daily move over the past 20 days, the coin rises over the next 1 to 2 days, and the larger that fall in units of its typical daily move, the larger the rise.
ideas.consequence: A sharp one-day drop relative to the coin's recent volatility is a reason to expect a short rebound, and a reason not to short into it.
